name: Refugio-Museo de la Guerra Civil, Cartagena
text: Cartagena was the Republic's main naval base and home of its fleet, which made it one of the most heavily bombed cities of the war. After a four-hour raid by the Condor Legion on 25 November 1936, the city began tunnelling shelters into its hills. This gallery, cut into the Cerro de la Concepción, was designed for more than 5,000 people and was still unfinished when Cartagena fell on 31 March 1939. Estimates of the number of raids the city suffered vary widely, from about 40 to 117. Opened as a museum in 2004, it covers daily life under the bombs, passive and active air defence (DECA), and the damage to the city. It is the best introduction to the war in the south-east.
look: A long tunnel in the hillside with exhibition rooms, photographs, air-raid sirens and audiovisuals; a panoramic lift beside it rises 45 m to the Castillo de la Concepción.
plan: Run by Cartagena Puerto de Culturas; entry is paid, and a combined ticket with other city museums is available. Entrance is on Calle Gisbert, in the centre, a 10-minute walk from the port.
disputed: The number of raids on Cartagena is given as anywhere from 40 to 117, depending on the source and on how raids are counted.

name: Refugio antiaéreo del Ayuntamiento, Valencia
text: From November 1936 to October 1937, Valencia was the seat of the Republican government, and it became a target. The first air raid came on 12 January 1937, and Italian bombers from Mallorca carried out most of the attacks that followed. The city dug more than 50 public shelters and adapted about 200 basements. In 1938 the architect José Luis Testor built this school shelter under the former Casa de la Enseñanza, next to the Town Hall, for 700 children. Five parallel vaulted chambers had ventilation, lighting and latrines. The Town Hall itself was bombed on 28 May 1937. The shelter was restored in 2016 and opened in 2017.
look: Five barrel-vaulted concrete chambers with original benches, restored signage, and panels on the bombing of Valencia and its shelter network.
plan: Free entry through the Town Hall exhibition hall at Calle Arzobispo Mayoral 1, closed Mondays. Official sources differ on whether it is open for free visits or only for Saturday guided tours, so check with the city museums (96 208 13 90) before going.
disputed: Totals for the bombing of Valencia vary. Tourism Valencia gives more than 440 raids, about 800 dead and 3,000 wounded; other counts differ.

name: Palau de Benicarló (seat of the Republican government)
text: When Madrid seemed about to fall in November 1936, the government of Francisco Largo Caballero left for Valencia. The city was the capital of the Republic until the government moved on to Barcelona in autumn 1937. This 15th-century Borja palace became the headquarters of the Presidency of the Republican government. The Cortes also sat in Valencia during this period, sharing the Town Hall. Here the Republic reorganised its army and dealt with the crisis of May 1937, when Juan Negrín replaced Largo Caballero. Valencia also hosted the Second International Congress of Writers for the Defence of Culture in July 1937. Since the 1980s the palace has been the seat of the Valencian parliament, the Corts Valencianes.
look: A Gothic–Renaissance palace facing Plaza de San Lorenzo. There is no Civil War display; the building itself is the point of interest.
plan: View from the square, a few minutes' walk from the Cathedral. The Corts run occasional guided tours; check their website.

name: Mercado Central, Alicante (bombing of 25 May 1938)
text: At 11:18 on 25 May 1938, Italian Aviazione Legionaria SM.79 bombers flying from Mallorca dropped about 90 bombs on central Alicante. There were seven to nine aircraft, led by Captains De Prato and Zigiotti. The morning market was crowded and the sirens had not sounded. It was one of the deadliest air raids of the war on a purely civilian target, and together with raids on Granollers and on British ships it caused protests in London. The square in front of the market was renamed Plaza 25 de Mayo in 2010, and the city holds a memorial act every year.
look: A ceramic plaque on the market wall and nine aluminium plaques in the square, one for each aircraft, which glow red at noon for ten minutes. Inside, the siren and a clock stopped at the time of the attack are preserved.
plan: The market is open Monday to Saturday mornings; the plaques can be seen at any time. It pairs with the Séneca shelter, 10 minutes away on foot.
disputed: Death toll: the Republican war report gives 250, cemetery records about 275, the municipal plaque 311, and a Francoist document 393. More than 1,000 people were wounded.

name: Port of Alicante – Stanbrook and the last refugees
text: As the Republic collapsed in March 1939, tens of thousands of Republican soldiers, officials and families converged on Alicante, hoping for evacuation by sea. On 28 March the British collier Stanbrook, under Captain Archibald Dickson, sailed for Oran carrying about 2,600–3,000 people, far beyond her capacity. Very few ships came after her. Between 15,000 and 20,000 people were left on the quays. Italian troops of the Littorio Division and Nationalist forces took the port, and on 1 April some of those trapped killed themselves rather than surrender. The rest were marched to the Los Almendros field and then to Albatera. The Generalitat Valenciana now marks 28 March as a day of remembrance.
look: Today a modern ferry and leisure port. A plaque to the Stanbrook's crew stands on the quayside (it was torn off once by vandals) and a street is named after the ship.
plan: Walk the waterfront from the Explanada. The plaque's exact position is not confirmed, so ask at the port tourist office. Combine with Los Almendros, 2 km north.
disputed: Stanbrook passengers are given as 2,638 by some sources and 'about 3,000' by others. Estimates of those left behind range from 15,000 to more than 20,000.

name: Campo de Los Almendros memorial, Alicante
text: Prisoners taken at Alicante port were held in an almond grove in La Goteta, about 3 km from the centre. The site was an open field of roughly 200 × 80 m ringed with barbed wire, with almost no food or water. For about a week from 31 March 1939 some 18,000–19,000 people were held here, though estimates run from 18,000 to 30,000. From here most were moved to Albatera or to prisons, and some were taken out and shot. The Nationalist army recorded 6,800 military prisoners. A campaign by the Alicante Vivo association led to a park named after the camp, opened in 2012, and a monument unveiled in 2014.
look: A small memorial monolith in a neighbourhood park on the former camp site. No original structures survive.
plan: Open public park; a 5-minute visit, near the MARQ archaeological museum and the Plaza Mar 2 centre.
disputed: Prisoner numbers range from 18,000 to 30,000, and deaths are estimated at anywhere from 600 to 2,000; there are no reliable records.

name: Refugio de la Plaza Séneca, Alicante
text: Alicante, a Republican port and supply base, was bombed repeatedly by Italian aircraft from Mallorca, most deadly on 25 May 1938. The city responded with public shelters under its squares. The Plaza Séneca shelter, next to the old bus station, is one of two (with Plaza Balmis) that the city now opens as a memory site. Soundscapes recreate the experience of a raid, and a linked exhibition, 'Alicante ha caído: aquí comienza la guerra', tells the story of the city's war and its end in the port.
look: Restored underground galleries with a sound and light installation recreating an air raid.
plan: Guided visits only; book online. Tours run on Wednesday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday in Spanish, Valencian and English, and cost about €5 (reduced €3). Check current times.

name: Línea XYZ – La Muela & La Vegatilla trenches, Jérica
text: After reaching the sea at Vinaròs in April 1938, Franco turned south towards Valencia. The Republic dug the Línea XYZ (or Matallana Line), a system of trenches, shelters and concrete bunkers about 150 km long, from Almenara on the coast to Santa Cruz de Moya. Between 18 and 24 July 1938, the forces of Varela, García Valiño, Solchaga and the Italian CTV attacked it. They broke against it less than 40 km from Valencia, and the Republican Ejército de Levante under General Menéndez held. Days later the Republic launched the Ebro offensive. Around Jérica, La Muela and La Vegatilla (Resistance Centre no. 7) were part of the rear line held by the 40th Division, and they survive very well.
look: Stone and excavated trenches, parapets, small shelters, machine-gun nests and concrete positions, some with Republican inscriptions, around La Muela and the Alto de Sayas.
plan: The waymarked 'Senda de las Trincheras' starts from the car park by the lavadero on Calle del Río in Jérica, about 13 km with climbs. The official La Muela–Aceitenebro route (12.3 km, about 3¼ h) starts from Novaliches. Wear boots and take water in summer.
disputed: Casualty figures are only estimates: Wikipedia gives about 20,000 Nationalist and 5,000 Republican. Beevor's view that the defence was a greater Republican victory than Guadalajara is an interpretation.

name: Línea XYZ at Viver – Morredondo, Cerro Cruz & El Ragudo bunkers
text: Viver lay at the centre of the Línea XYZ, where the Nationalist drive down the Teruel–Sagunto road and railway was stopped in July 1938. Republican engineers used the broken terrain rather than building a continuous wall. The result was a network of trenches, shelters and bunkers covering the road and the railway pass at El Ragudo. Although the Nationalists had more men and command of the air, repeated frontal assaults here failed. The town has signposted short walks to the Morredondo trenches and the Cerro Cruz defensive position, and the official Línea XYZ project maps a route to the Ragudo bunkers (Viver–Benafer).
look: Trenches at Morredondo, fortified positions on the Cerro Cruz, and concrete bunkers and railway ruins at El Ragudo.
plan: Morredondo and Cerro Cruz are each about an hour's walk from Viver. El Ragudo is reached along the Ojos Negros greenway or by track. A local interpretation centre (CIBAL) and guided tours have been reported; check with Viver town hall.

name: Sierra de Espadán – Las Tetas & La Ràpita positions
text: On the eastern part of the Línea XYZ, García Valiño's corps tried to break through the Sierra de Espadán via the Veo valley and seize the heights of La Ràpita and Espadà, which anchored the Republican line. After bombardment from 10 July 1938, the Nationalists took one of the two 'Tetas' summits on 18 July. Heavy fighting on 19 and 23 July failed to take the main ridge. The 1st Navarrese Division, left exposed on the captured hill, fortified it with bunkers and concrete walls. Both sides' works survive on the mountain.
look: Stepped parapets with loopholes, bunkers, trenches cut into the rock on La Ràpita's north-east slope, and stone sniper posts near the 1,106 m summit, with wide views over the Espadán.
plan: Official circular route 'Las Tetas i la Ràpita': 10 km, 702 m ascent, about 3½ h, with a demanding first half. It starts from the Alcudia de Veo / Algimia de Almonacid area. For experienced walkers only.

name: Paredón de España (El Terrer), Paterna
text: After Valencia fell in March 1939, the Franco regime used the wall of a former quarry beside Paterna cemetery, known as El Terrer or the 'Paredón de España', as its main execution site in the province. Records document 2,238 people shot here between 1939 and 1956 and buried in mass graves 65 to 135 of the neighbouring cemetery. About 94% came from the Valencian region. The graves have been the focus of exhumations driven largely by victims' relatives, many of them women. The adjacent cemetery now holds the '2238' memorial listing the names. This is the most important site of post-war repression in the Valencian Community.
look: The bullet-scarred wall with a monument and plaques; in Paterna municipal cemetery nearby, the mass-grave area and the 2238 memorial.
plan: The wall is in the open near the cemetery and a school sports hall; the cemetery keeps normal daytime hours. Please behave respectfully, as families still visit.

name: Albatera concentration camp memorial, San Isidro
text: The Republic built this camp near San Isidro in 1937 as a labour camp. It held around 1,000 prisoners, including many detainees suspected of Nationalist sympathies, who drained the Saladares marshes; five deaths were reported. After April 1939 the victors turned it into a concentration camp for Republicans taken at Alicante port and Los Almendros. Estimates run from 12,000 to 30,000 inmates. Hunger, lice and disease killed many, with 138 deaths recorded in April 1939 alone, and prisoners were removed for execution ('sacas'). Among those held were the poet Marcos Ana and the jurist Manuel García-Pelayo. The camp closed in October 1939. Excavations began in 2020.
look: A 1995 memorial of iron beams and chains near the station, a palm grove on the camp site, and one surviving original building (a former watchtower, now a shed). Excavation areas may be visible.
plan: The memorial is freely accessible near San Isidro station, 3 km from Albatera; the site itself is largely farmland. An interpretation centre is planned.
disputed: The number of prisoners in 1939 is uncertain because the records were destroyed; estimates range from about 7,000 to 30,000.

name: Batería de Castillitos, Cabo Tiñoso (Cartagena)
text: Cartagena's coast was guarded by a ring of modern batteries. Castillitos, built between 1933 and 1936 in a mock-castle style, mounted two Vickers 381 mm guns with a range of about 35 km. It is reported to have fired only once in the war, in 1937. The batteries of Cabo Tiñoso played their decisive part at the very end. After the anti-Negrín uprising in Cartagena of 4–7 March 1939, the Republican fleet left for Bizerte. A Nationalist relief convoy then approached the port after troops loyal to the Republic had retaken the batteries. On 7 March 1939, a 152 mm shell from the neighbouring La Parajola battery hit the transport Castillo de Olite. Of 2,112 men aboard, 1,476 died, making it Spain's deadliest shipwreck.
look: Monumental gun emplacements with both 381 mm barrels still in place, tunnels, magazines and fake-castle towers on a clifftop 250 m above the sea.
plan: Drive the narrow, winding military road from Campillo de Adentro to the car park; the site is free and open (Ministry of Defence property, partly restored in 2010–11). Allow time for the walk and the views; not for anyone afraid of heights.
disputed: The claim that Castillitos fired only once, in 1937, comes from secondary tourism sources.

name: Refugio antiaéreo de la Plaza Tetuán, Castelló de la Plana
text: Castelló was bombed by Nationalist and Italian aircraft as the front approached in spring 1938, and it fell to Nationalist troops in June 1938 during the drive towards Valencia. This public shelter under Plaza Tetuán was built in 1937–38 to protect the townspeople. Restored and opened as a site of the city museum (MUCC), it presents the war as civilians lived it: the raids, the sirens and the shelter network, and life in a city that changed hands in the middle of the war.
look: A restored underground shelter with exhibits and multimedia; audioguides in Spanish, Valencian, English and French.
plan: Free entry; open Tuesday to Saturday 16:00–19:00 and Sunday 10:00–14:00, closed Mondays and in heavy rain. Guided tour at 19:00 (book on 964 73 52 17). Self-guided visit about 45 minutes, maximum 60 people inside.

name: Porto Cristo – Bayo's landing on Mallorca
text: Mallorca sided with the coup in July 1936. On 16 August Captain Alberto Bayo, with Catalan and Valencian militia and naval support, landed on the east coast at Porto Cristo and Punta Amer (Sa Coma), renaming the port 'Porto Rojo'. The attackers were poorly coordinated, and the defenders were reinforced by Italian aircraft and the Fascist Arconovaldo Bonaccorsi ('Conde Rossi'). The counter-attack from 27 August drove the Republicans back, and they re-embarked by 4 September, leaving equipment behind. Captured militiamen and local leftists were executed; in 2020 excavations at Son Coletes cemetery in Manacor found remains of milicianos and two nurses.
look: The harbour and beaches of Porto Cristo and Sa Coma, where the landing and fighting took place. There is no major monument on the shore; Son Coletes cemetery in Manacor has the excavated grave site.
plan: Walk the harbour and the Passeig de la Sirena, then drive 12 km to Manacor for Son Coletes cemetery. Pairs with a visit to the Drach caves.
disputed: Sources disagree on the end date of the operation: some give 4 September and Wikipedia gives 12 September 1936.

name: Es Campament penal colony, La Savina (Formentera)
text: After the war the Franco regime set up a penal colony for Republican prisoners on Formentera, beside the road from La Savina to La Mola. Some 2,133 men passed through it, many of them from mainland Spain and the Canaries. On 1 January 1942 it held 1,209 prisoners, on an island of about 3,000 inhabitants. At least 58 died of hunger and disease between 1941 and its closure in November 1942, and they were buried in Sant Francesc cemetery, where the Fòrum per la Memòria has exhumed remains. The site was declared a Bien de Interés Cultural in 2014, and the protection was upheld in court in 2018.
look: Low perimeter walls, barracks foundations, wells and a plaque with Joan Coromines' poem 'The Cemetery of the Living', beside the main road near the Estany des Peix.
plan: Seen from the PM-820 about 1 km out of La Savina port. Remains are fragmentary and luxury flats stand next to it, so stay on public land.
disputed: Sources give 1,400 as the usual capacity and 2,133 as the total number who passed through; do not confuse the two figures.

name: Refugio de la calle Serranos, Valencia
text: One of more than 50 public shelters built in Valencia against the raids, which Italian bombers based in Mallorca carried out from 1937 to 1939. Begun on 22 June 1937 at Calle Serranos 25, beside the medieval Torres de Serranos, it held about 400 people in three reinforced-concrete chambers under a roof more than 1.5 m thick. With the shelters at Calle Alta (Falla Ripalda–Sogueros), Bombas Gens and Massarrojos, it forms part of the city's network of visitable shelters. Their Art Deco 'REFUGIO' lettering has become an emblem of Valencia's wartime design.
look: Three concrete chambers with original features and interpretation panels.
plan: Free guided visits on Tuesday and Saturday mornings plus Tuesday afternoons, by reservation on 962 081 390.
disputed: The Mapcarta point is labelled only 'old civil war bomb shelter', 120 m from the Torres de Serranos. It is very probably, but not certainly, the Calle Serranos 25 shelter.
